source.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ מֵאַ֣חֲרֵי כֵ֔ן וַיַּ֤עַשׂ לוֹ֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם מֶרְכָּבָ֖ה וְסֻסִ֑ים וַחֲמִשִּׁ֥ים אִ֖ישׁ רָצִ֥ים לְפָנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was after thus, and made for himself Absalom a chariot and horses, and fifty men running before him.

en.L: And it happened after this that Absalom made for himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men running before him.
en.B: Some time after this, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him.
en.R: Some time later, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses. He also had fifty men who ran in front of him wherever he went.

decisions.choice: a chariot, horses and runners: the display of a king
decisions.reason: A chariot with men running ahead of it was the mark of a king (1 Samuel 8:11). Adonijah does the same when he reaches for the throne (1 Kings 1:5). Israel's kings had hardly used horses and chariots until now (8:4), so Absalom's show of royal state would be noticed by everyone.

decisions.choice: after this: after Absalom was restored to the king
decisions.reason: The phrase links this chapter to the end of chapter 14, where David at last received Absalom back and kissed him (14:33).

decisions.choice: ran in front of him wherever he went
decisions.reason: Readable adds "wherever he went" to make plain that the runners were a standing escort, not a single event.

source.text: וְהִשְׁכִּים֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם וְעָמַ֕ד עַל־יַ֖ד דֶּ֣רֶךְ הַשָּׁ֑עַר וַיְהִ֡י כָּל־הָאִ֣ישׁ אֲשֶֽׁר־יִהְיֶה־לּוֹ־רִיב֩ לָב֨וֹא אֶל־הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לַמִּשְׁפָּ֗ט וַיִּקְרָ֨א אַבְשָׁל֤וֹם אֵלָיו֙ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵֽי־מִזֶּ֥ה עִיר֙ אַ֔תָּה וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מֵאַחַ֥ד שִׁבְטֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And rose early Absalom and stood beside [the] road of the gate; and it was, every man who had a dispute to come to the king for judgment, and called Absalom to him and said, From where [is] this city [of] you? And he said, From one [of the] tribes of Israel [is] your servant.

en.L: And Absalom would rise early and stand beside the road of the gate; and whenever any man had a dispute to come to the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city [are] you?" And he would say, "Your servant [is] from one of the tribes of Israel."
en.B: Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road that led to the city gate. Whenever anyone had a dispute to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him, "What town are you from?" And he would answer, "Your servant is from such and such a tribe of Israel."
en.R: Absalom used to get up early and stand beside the road into the city gate. People came that way when they had a dispute and wanted the king to decide it. Absalom would call out to such a person, "What town are you from?" The man would answer, "Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel," and he would name his tribe.

decisions.choice: the road of the gate: the way in to the city gate, where cases were heard
decisions.reason: The gate of a city was where the elders sat and where disputes were settled (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-2). A king also gave judgment there (19:9). Absalom stood where people with complaints would pass on their way to the king.

decisions.choice: Absalom would rise early ... would call: what he did again and again
decisions.reason: The verb forms describe a habit over a long time, not one morning. Verse 7 says how long it went on.

decisions.choice: from one of the tribes of Israel: from such and such a tribe
decisions.reason: The writer gives the man's answer in general form; each man would name his own tribe. The point is that the people came from the northern tribes as well as Judah, the people Absalom won over (verse 6).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "I"
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as "your servant" was ordinary courtesy toward a person of rank (Genesis 18:3; 1 Samuel 20:7-8). The man treats Absalom as a great man, perhaps already as a prince who can act for the king.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel 20, the polite self-reference stays "your servant" at every level, so that the courtesy of the speech is kept.

decisions.choice: such and such a tribe
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "such and such a tribe" to show that the answer is a summary (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: and he would name his tribe
decisions.reason: Readable adds that each man named his tribe, which is what the general wording means.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם רְאֵ֥ה דְבָרֶ֖ךָ טוֹבִ֣ים וּנְכֹחִ֑ים וְשֹׁמֵ֥עַ אֵין־לְךָ֖ מֵאֵ֥ת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Absalom, See, your matters [are] good and right, and one hearing there is not for you from the king.

en.L: And Absalom would say to him, "See, your matters [are] good and right, but there is no one hearing [them] for you from the king."
en.B: Absalom would say to him, "Look, your claims are good and right, but there is no one from the king to hear your case."
en.R: Then Absalom would say to him, "Look, you are right, and you have a good case. But the king has no one to listen to you."

decisions.choice: your matters are good and right: your case is sound
decisions.reason: "Matters" (literally "words") are the man's claims in his dispute. Absalom agrees with every man before hearing the other side, which is the opposite of judging fairly (Deuteronomy 1:16-17).

decisions.choice: no one hearing for you from the king: no officer appointed by the king to hear cases
decisions.reason: "From the king" means someone the king has appointed. Absalom blames the king for neglect, whether or not it was true.

decisions.choice: listen to you
decisions.reason: Readable uses "listen" for the hearing of a legal case, the plainer word.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם מִי־יְשִׂמֵ֥נִי שֹׁפֵ֖ט בָּאָ֑רֶץ וְעָלַ֗י יָב֥וֹא כָּל־אִ֛ישׁ אֲשֶֽׁר־יִהְיֶה־לּוֹ־רִ֥יב וּמִשְׁפָּ֖ט וְהִצְדַּקְתִּֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Absalom, Who will make me judge in the land, and to me would come every man who has a dispute and judgment, and I would do him justice?

en.L: And Absalom would say, "Who will make me judge in the land, so that every man who has a dispute or case could come to me, and I would give him justice?"
en.B: Absalom would also say, "If only someone would make me judge in the land! Then anyone with a dispute or a case could come to me, and I would see that justice is done."
en.R: Absalom would also say, "I wish someone would make me the judge in this land! Then anyone with a problem or a court case could come to me. I would make sure they got justice."

decisions.choice: who will make me judge?: a wish, "if only I were made judge"
decisions.reason: "Who will ...?" is a common Hebrew way of expressing a wish (23:15; Numbers 11:4). Absalom does not ask for an answer; he lets people know what he would do in power.

decisions.choice: judge: one who decides cases, a duty of the king
decisions.reason: Judging the people was one of the king's chief tasks (8:15; 1 Samuel 8:5, 20). By wishing to be judge, Absalom is wishing to rule.

decisions.choice: I would do him justice: declare him in the right, give him his rights
decisions.reason: The verb means to declare someone in the right in a dispute (Deuteronomy 25:1). Absalom promises everyone a win.

decisions.choice: anyone
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "every man" means every person who brought a case. Balanced and Readable say "anyone", and Readable "they" afterwards; Literal keeps "every man" and "him".

source.text: וְהָיָה֙ בִּקְרָב־אִ֔ישׁ לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֖ת ל֑וֹ וְשָׁלַ֧ח אֶת־יָד֛וֹ וְהֶחֱזִ֥יק ל֖וֹ וְנָ֥שַׁק לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when came near a man to bow down to him, and he put out his hand and took hold of him and kissed him.

en.L: And whenever a man came near to bow down to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.
en.B: And whenever anyone approached to bow low before him, Absalom would stretch out his hand, take hold of the man and kiss him.
en.R: When someone came up to bow down to him, Absalom would not allow it. He would reach out his hand, take hold of the person and kiss him.

decisions.choice: he took hold of him and kissed him: he refused the honor and treated him as an equal
decisions.reason: Bowing to the ground was the respect owed to the king and his family (14:4, 33). Absalom stops it and greets the man with a kiss, as a friend. He makes himself seem humble and warm, in contrast to the king's distance.

decisions.choice: Absalom would not allow it
decisions.reason: Readable says outright what the gesture meant: Absalom stopped the man from bowing. This is implied by the Hebrew, not stated.

decisions.choice: anyone; someone
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "a man" means any person. Balanced and Readable use the general word.

source.text: וַיַּ֨עַשׂ אַבְשָׁל֜וֹם כַּדָּבָ֤ר הַזֶּה֙ לְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁר־יָבֹ֥אוּ לַמִּשְׁפָּ֖ט אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיְגַנֵּב֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם אֶת־לֵ֖ב אַנְשֵׁ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And did Absalom according to this word to all Israel who came for judgment to the king, and stole Absalom the heart of [the] men of Israel.

en.L: And Absalom did according to this manner to all Israel who came to the king for judgment; and Absalom stole the heart of the men of Israel.
en.B: Absalom acted this way toward every Israelite who came to the king for judgment. In this way Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
en.R: Absalom treated in this way all the Israelites who came to ask the king for justice. And so he stole the loyalty of the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: stole the heart: won their loyalty by deceit
decisions.reason: To "steal the heart" of someone is to deceive him (Genesis 31:20, 26, where Jacob "stole the heart" of Laban). Here it means both that Absalom won the people's affection and that he did it by trickery: the people gave him the loyalty that belonged to their king.

decisions.choice: all Israel; the men of Israel: the people of the whole nation
decisions.reason: "All Israel" and "the men of Israel" mean the Israelites in general, the people of the tribes who came with cases (verse 2), not only Judah.

decisions.choice: stole the loyalty
decisions.reason: Readable says "loyalty" for "heart", since the idiom is about allegiance, and keeps "stole" for the deceit.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people of Israel" for "the men of Israel", since the phrase means the nation as a whole (meaning decision m2).

source.text: וַיְהִ֕י מִקֵּ֖ץ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֵ֣לֲכָה נָּ֗א וַאֲשַׁלֵּ֛ם אֶת־נִדְרִ֛י אֲשֶׁר־נָדַ֥רְתִּי לַֽיהוָ֖ה בְּחֶבְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was at [the] end of forty years, and said Absalom to the king, Let me go, please, and let me pay my vow that I vowed to Yahweh in Hebron.

en.L: And it happened at the end of forty years that Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow that I vowed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Hebron.
en.B: When forty years had come to an end, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: After forty years, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron. I want to do what I promised {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} I would do.

decisions.choice: forty years: as the Hebrew text reads
decisions.reason: The standard Hebrew text says "forty years". Some manuscripts of the Greek translation, the Syriac translation and the Jewish historian Josephus read "four years". Forty years is hard to fit: David reigned forty years in all (5:4), and this is not the end of his reign. If "forty" is right, the count must start from some earlier point, such as David's anointing by Samuel (1 Samuel 16:13) or Absalom's birth. "Four years" would count from Absalom's return to Jerusalem (14:28, where he had lived there two years before seeing the king), which fits the story well; in Hebrew writing the two numbers could be confused. The Hebrew reading is kept here, but the question is open.

decisions.choice: pay my vow: carry out what one has promised God, usually with a sacrifice
decisions.reason: A vow was a promise to give God something, often an offering, if he answered a prayer (Genesis 28:20-22; 1 Samuel 1:11). Paying it was a duty (Deuteronomy 23:22-24). Absalom's vow is described in verse 8.

decisions.choice: Hebron: David's first royal city and Absalom's birthplace
decisions.reason: David was first made king in Hebron and reigned there seven and a half years (2:1-4, 11; 5:1-5). Absalom was born there (3:2-3). It was a natural place to rally people who missed the old days, or who resented the move to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: let me go to Hebron
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable move "Hebron" next to "go", where English expects a destination; the Hebrew puts it at the end, after the vow.

decisions.choice: do what I promised the LORD I would do
decisions.reason: Readable explains "pay my vow" in everyday words.

source.text: כִּי־נֵ֨דֶר֙ נָדַ֣ר עַבְדְּךָ֔ בְּשִׁבְתִּ֥י בִגְשׁ֛וּר בַּאֲרָ֖ם לֵאמֹ֑ר אִם־יָשׁ֨וֹב יְשִׁיבֵ֤נִי יְהוָה֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְעָבַדְתִּ֖י אֶת־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: For a vow vowed your servant when I lived in Geshur in Aram, saying, If indeed will bring me back Yahweh [to] Jerusalem, then I will serve Yahweh.

en.L: For your servant vowed a vow while I lived in Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} indeed brings me back [to] Jerusalem, then I will serve {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.B: For your servant made a vow while I was living at Geshur in Aram. I said, 'If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} really brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.R: While your servant was living in Geshur in Aram, I made a promise. I said, 'If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} really brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} with an offering.'"

decisions.choice: if the LORD indeed brings me back: the reading noted in the margin
alternatives: if indeed I dwell, and the LORD brings me back
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell the first verb so that it could be read "if he indeed dwells", and the reading noted by the scribes in the margin gives the form of "bring back", making a doubled verb for emphasis: "if he indeed brings me back". The second reading fits the sentence and is followed here; the sense is hardly affected.

decisions.choice: serve the LORD: worship him with sacrifice
decisions.reason: "Serve" here means an act of worship, as in Exodus 3:12 and 10:26. The sacrifices of verse 12 were this worship. Some Greek manuscripts add "in Hebron", which is what Absalom means in verse 7.

decisions.choice: Geshur in Aram: the small kingdom of Absalom's mother's family
decisions.reason: Geshur lay east of the Sea of Galilee, among the Aramean peoples. Absalom's mother was the daughter of its king Talmai, and Absalom fled there after killing Amnon and stayed three years (3:3; 13:37-38).

decisions.choice: your servant: polite self-reference
decisions.reason: As in verse 2. Absalom speaks to his father as a humble subject while planning to take his throne.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, "your servant" is kept at every level; it is followed by "I", as in the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: worship (Readable: worship ... with an offering)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "worship" for "serve" (meaning decision m2); Readable adds "with an offering" to show what the worship involved.

source.text: וַיֹּֽאמֶר־ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֵ֣ךְ בְּשָׁל֑וֹם וַיָּ֖קָם וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ חֶבְרֽוֹנָה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And said to him the king, Go in peace. And he arose and went to Hebron.

en.L: And the king said to him, "Go in peace." And he arose and went to Hebron.
en.B: The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he got up and went to Hebron.
en.R: The king told him, "Go, and may all be well with you." So Absalom left and went to Hebron.

decisions.choice: go in peace: a farewell blessing
decisions.reason: The words send someone off with good wishes (1 Samuel 1:17; 20:42). These are the last words the story gives from David to Absalom. David blesses the journey that begins the revolt against him.

decisions.choice: may all be well with you
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the blessing in "go in peace".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ מְרַגְּלִ֔ים בְּכָל־שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר כְּשָׁמְעֲכֶם֙ אֶת־ק֣וֹל הַשֹּׁפָ֔ר וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֕ם מָלַ֥ךְ אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם בְּחֶבְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent Absalom spies through all [the] tribes of Israel, saying, As you hear the sound of the horn, and you will say, Has become king Absalom in Hebron.

en.L: And Absalom sent spies through all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, you will say, 'Absalom has become king in Hebron!'"
en.B: Meanwhile Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel to say, "As soon as you hear the sound of the ram's horn, say, 'Absalom has become king in Hebron!'"
en.R: Absalom also sent men secretly to all the tribes of Israel. They told the people, "When you hear the trumpet blow, shout, 'Absalom is now king in Hebron!'"

decisions.choice: spies: secret agents
decisions.reason: The word usually means spies sent to look over a land (Joshua 2:1). Here they are agents who go secretly to prepare people for the signal.

decisions.choice: the sound of the horn: the signal for a public event
decisions.reason: The ram's horn was blown to call people together, for war or for the crowning of a king (1 Kings 1:34, 39; 2 Kings 9:13). Its sound would pass from town to town.

decisions.choice: Absalom has become king: the cry that proclaims a new king
decisions.reason: The verb says that a reign has begun, as in the cry for Jehu (2 Kings 9:13). The same kind of cry is heard when Solomon is made king (1 Kings 1:11, 18).

decisions.choice: ram's horn (Literal and Readable: trumpet)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel 13:3, Balanced names the instrument, while Literal and Readable use the familiar word "trumpet".

decisions.choice: secret messengers; sent men secretly
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable describe what these "spies" did, since they did not gather information but spread a message.

source.text: וְאֶת־אַבְשָׁל֗וֹם הָלְכ֞וּ מָאתַ֤יִם אִישׁ֙ מִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם קְרֻאִ֖ים וְהֹלְכִ֣ים לְתֻמָּ֑ם וְלֹ֥א יָדְע֖וּ כָּל־דָּבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And with Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem, invited, and going in their innocence, and not they knew any thing.

en.L: And with Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem, invited, and going in their innocence, and they did not know anything.
en.B: Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited as guests and went in all innocence, knowing nothing about the plot.
en.R: Two hundred men from Jerusalem went along with Absalom. They had been invited to the feast, and they had no idea what he was planning.

decisions.choice: invited: guests for the sacrificial meal
decisions.reason: A sacrifice of this kind was followed by a feast, and guests were invited to it (1 Samuel 9:13, 22; 16:3-5; 1 Kings 1:9, 25). The presence of leading men from Jerusalem would make it look as if the capital supported Absalom.

decisions.choice: going in their innocence: without any knowledge of the plan
decisions.reason: "In their innocence" means simply, without guile or suspicion. They did not know what the feast was for.

decisions.choice: about the plot; what he was planning
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the men did not know, which the Hebrew leaves as "anything".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח אַ֠בְשָׁלוֹם אֶת־אֲחִיתֹ֨פֶל הַגִּֽילֹנִ֜י יוֹעֵ֣ץ דָּוִ֗ד מֵֽעִירוֹ֙ מִגִּלֹ֔ה בְּזָבְח֖וֹ אֶת־הַזְּבָחִ֑ים וַיְהִ֤י הַקֶּ֨שֶׁר֙ אַמִּ֔ץ וְהָעָ֛ם הוֹלֵ֥ךְ וָרָ֖ב אֶת־אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent Absalom [for] Ahithophel the Gilonite, counselor of David, from his city, from Giloh, while he offered the sacrifices; and was the conspiracy strong, and the people going and increasing with Absalom.

en.L: And Absalom sent [for] Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city, from Giloh, while he was offering the sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
en.B: While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he also sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his town of Giloh. So the conspiracy grew strong, and the number of people supporting Absalom kept increasing.
en.R: While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel from his hometown of Giloh. Ahithophel had been one of David's advisers. The plot became stronger, and more and more people joined Absalom's side.

decisions.choice: sent for Ahithophel from his city: summoned him from Giloh
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says Absalom "sent Ahithophel ... from his city", which in this setting means he sent and brought him from Giloh to Hebron. Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:51), not far from Hebron.

decisions.choice: Ahithophel, David's counselor: the king's most trusted adviser
decisions.reason: Ahithophel's advice was treated as if it were a word from God (16:23). His son Eliam was one of David's mighty men (23:34), and Bathsheba was the daughter of an Eliam (11:3), so Ahithophel may have been her grandfather. That would help explain why he turned against David.

decisions.choice: while he was offering: Absalom, at Hebron
decisions.reason: "He" is Absalom, whose sacrifices were the pretext for the journey (verses 7-8).

decisions.choice: the people kept increasing with Absalom: more and more supporters
decisions.reason: "The people" here are the Israelites who took Absalom's side, not an army as yet. The Hebrew "going and increasing" describes steady growth.

decisions.choice: Ahithophel had been one of David's advisers
decisions.reason: Readable says in a separate sentence who Ahithophel was, and drops the clan name "the Gilonite", which repeats "from Giloh".

source.text: וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּגִּ֔יד אֶל־דָּוִ֖ד לֵאמֹ֑ר הָיָ֛ה לֶב־אִ֥ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַחֲרֵ֥י אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: And came the messenger to David, saying, Is [the] heart of [the] men of Israel after Absalom.

en.L: And the messenger came to David, saying, "The heart of the men of Israel is after Absalom."
en.B: A messenger came to David and said, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone over to Absalom."
en.R: Someone came to David with this news: "The people of Israel have turned to Absalom. They want him as their leader now."

decisions.choice: the heart is after Absalom: their loyalty follows him
decisions.reason: To be "after" someone is to follow him as leader (2:10; 1 Kings 12:20). The heart that Absalom stole (verse 6) has now gone over to him.

decisions.choice: the messenger: one who brought the news
decisions.reason: The article points to the one who came with this report, as in 1 Samuel 4:17, without giving his name.

decisions.choice: They want him as their leader now
decisions.reason: Readable adds a sentence to explain the idiom "the heart is after".

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, Readable says "the people of Israel" for the nation as a whole.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּ֠וִד לְכָל־עֲבָדָ֨יו אֲשֶׁר־אִתּ֤וֹ בִירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ ק֣וּמוּ וְנִבְרָ֔חָה כִּ֛י לֹא־תִֽהְיֶה־לָּ֥נוּ פְלֵיטָ֖ה מִפְּנֵ֣י אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם מַהֲר֣וּ לָלֶ֗כֶת פֶּן־יְמַהֵ֤ר וְהִשִּׂגָ֨נוּ֙ וְהִדִּ֤יחַ עָלֵ֨ינוּ֙ אֶת־הָ֣רָעָ֔ה וְהִכָּ֥ה הָעִ֖יר לְפִי־חָֽרֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: And said David to all his servants who [were] with him in Jerusalem, Arise and let us flee, for not there will be for us escape from before Absalom; hurry to go, lest he hurry and overtake us and bring down on us the disaster, and strike the city by [the] mouth of [the] sword.

en.L: And David said to all his servants who [were] with him in Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, for there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Hurry to go, lest he hurry and overtake us and bring down disaster on us and strike the city with the mouth of the sword."
en.B: Then David said to all his officials who were with him in Jerusalem, "Get up! We must flee, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Leave at once, or he will move quickly, overtake us, bring disaster on us and put the city to the sword."
en.R: Then David said to all his officials who were with him in Jerusalem, "Come on! We have to run away, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Go quickly! If we do not, he will soon catch us. He will bring disaster on us, and his men will kill the people of the city."

decisions.choice: let us flee: David decides to leave the city at once
decisions.reason: David does not wait to fight in Jerusalem. He fears that Absalom will come quickly from Hebron, about a day's march away, and that a battle inside the city would destroy it. Leaving also gives him time to gather his forces (17:1-2, 21-22).

decisions.choice: strike the city with the mouth of the sword: kill its people
decisions.reason: "The mouth of the sword" is its edge, pictured as a mouth that devours (11:25; Deuteronomy 13:16). To strike a city this way is to put its people to death.

decisions.choice: bring down disaster on us: bring ruin on David's household and men
decisions.reason: The verb pictures disaster being driven or thrust down on them. It is the ruin of David and those loyal to him.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: As with "the king's servants" elsewhere in these books, Balanced and Readable say "officials" for the men of David's court; Literal keeps "servants".

decisions.choice: his men will kill the people of the city
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom "strike with the mouth of the sword".

source.text: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ עַבְדֵֽי־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ כְּכֹ֧ל אֲשֶׁר־יִבְחַ֛ר אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ הִנֵּ֥ה עֲבָדֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] servants of the king to the king, According to all that will choose my lord the king, here [are] your servants.

en.L: And the king's servants said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king chooses, here [are] your servants."
en.B: The king's officials said to the king, "Whatever my lord the king decides, your servants are ready."
en.R: The king's officials answered, "Your servants are ready to do whatever our master the king decides."

decisions.choice: here are your servants: we are ready to serve
decisions.reason: The phrase is the same kind of answer as "Here I am" (1 Samuel 3:4): a statement of readiness to obey. Calling themselves "your servants" is the polite form of "we".

decisions.choice: your servants
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, polite self-reference stays "your servants" at every level. In the narrator's words the same men are "the king's servants" (Literal) or "officials" (verse 14).

decisions.choice: our master
decisions.reason: Readable says "our master" for "my lord", since the officials speak together; Literal and Balanced keep the court phrase "my lord the king".

source.text: וַיֵּצֵ֥א הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וְכָל־בֵּית֖וֹ בְּרַגְלָ֑יו וַיַּעֲזֹ֣ב הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ אֵ֣ת עֶ֧שֶׂר נָשִׁ֛ים פִּֽלַגְשִׁ֖ים לִשְׁמֹ֥ר הַבָּֽיִת׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out the king and all his household at his feet; and left the king ten women, concubines, to keep the house.

en.L: And the king went out, and all his household [went] at his feet; and the king left ten women, concubines, to keep the house.
en.B: So the king set out, with all his household following him. But he left ten concubines behind to look after the palace.
en.R: So the king left, and all his family went with him. But he left ten of his concubines (secondary wives) behind to take care of the palace.

decisions.choice: at his feet: following him
decisions.reason: To go "at someone's feet" is to go behind him as a follower (Judges 4:10; 8:5).

decisions.choice: concubines: wives of lower rank
decisions.reason: A concubine was a wife of secondary status, often without a bride price or the full rights of a wife (Genesis 25:6; Judges 19:1). A king's concubines belonged to his household, and taking them was a claim to his throne (3:7; 12:8).

decisions.choice: left ten concubines to keep the house: preparing for 16:21-22
decisions.reason: These women will be taken by Absalom in public on Ahithophel's advice (16:21-22), fulfilling Nathan's word that someone close to David would lie with his wives in broad daylight (12:11-12). David later shuts them away for the rest of their lives (20:3).

decisions.choice: the palace
decisions.reason: "The house" is the king's house. Balanced and Readable say "the palace".

decisions.choice: concubines (secondary wives)
decisions.reason: As in Judges, Readable explains "concubine" at its first use in the chapter.

source.text: וַיֵּצֵ֥א הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וְכָל־הָעָ֖ם בְּרַגְלָ֑יו וַיַּעַמְד֖וּ בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּרְחָֽק׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out the king and all the people at his feet, and they stood [at the] house of the distance.

en.L: And the king went out, and all the people at his feet, and they stopped at the far house.
en.B: So the king went out with all the people following him, and they stopped at the last house.
en.R: The king went out, and all the people followed him. They stopped at the last house at the edge of the city.

decisions.choice: the far house: the last house on the way out of the city
decisions.reason: The Hebrew means "the house of the distance", probably the last house before the open country, where the king stopped to let his people pass him (verse 18). It could also be the name of a place, Beth-merhak, but no such place is known elsewhere.

decisions.choice: all the people: those who left with David
decisions.reason: "The people" here are everyone who went with the king: his household, his officials and his soldiers (verse 18).

decisions.choice: at the edge of the city
decisions.reason: Readable adds where the last house stood, which is implied by the scene.

source.text: וְכָל־עֲבָדָיו֙ עֹבְרִ֣ים עַל־יָד֔וֹ וְכָל־הַכְּרֵתִ֖י וְכָל־הַפְּלֵתִ֑י וְכָֽל־הַגִּתִּ֞ים שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֣וֹת אִ֗ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֤אוּ בְרַגְלוֹ֙ מִגַּ֔ת עֹבְרִ֖ים עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And all his servants [were] passing by at his side, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who came at his foot from Gath, [were] passing by before the king.

en.L: And all his servants [were] passing by beside him, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites; and all the Gittites, six hundred men who had come at his feet from Gath, [were] passing by before the king.
en.B: All his officials marched past him, with every one of the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And all the Gittites, the six hundred men who had followed him from Gath, marched past the king.
en.R: All his officials walked past him, along with the Cherethites and the Pelethites, who were the king's bodyguard. Then all six hundred men from Gath who had followed him from there went past the king.

decisions.choice: Cherethites and Pelethites: foreign soldiers who formed the king's guard
decisions.reason: As in 8:18. The names are those of peoples, not of ranks or duties: the Cherethites came from the Philistine coast and were linked with Crete (1 Samuel 30:14), and the Pelethites were probably Philistines too. They were loyal to David alone (20:7; 1 Kings 1:38, 44).

decisions.choice: who had come at his feet from Gath: who followed him from Gath
alternatives: David's six hundred men from his time at Gath
decisions.reason: "His" most naturally means the man the next verses speak of, Ittai: these are Gittites, men of Gath, who came with him (verses 19-22). But since the king has just been named, "his" may also mean David. When David lived at Gath he had six hundred men with him (1 Samuel 27:2-3), and some think these are that old company. The Hebrew can be read either way, and the rendering keeps "him".

decisions.choice: passing by before the king: marching past him in review
decisions.reason: The king stood at the last house while his household and soldiers filed past him (verse 17). It was both an inspection and a sign of who stood by him.

decisions.choice: who were the king's bodyguard
decisions.reason: As in 8:18, Readable says who the Cherethites and Pelethites were.

decisions.choice: six hundred men from Gath
decisions.reason: Readable says "men from Gath" for "Gittites", the plainer form of the name.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: As in verse 14.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־אִתַּ֣י הַגִּתִּ֔י לָ֧מָּה תֵלֵ֛ךְ גַּם־אַתָּ֖ה אִתָּ֑נוּ שׁ֣וּב וְשֵׁ֤ב עִם־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ כִּֽי־נָכְרִ֣י אַ֔תָּה וְגַם־גֹּלֶ֥ה אַתָּ֖ה לִמְקוֹמֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Why will you go also you with us? Return and stay with the king, for a foreigner [are] you and also an exile [are] you to your place.

en.L: And the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why will you also go with us? Return and stay with the king, for you [are] a foreigner, and also you [are] an exile from your place.
en.B: Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why should you come with us too? Go back and stay with the king. You are a foreigner, and an exile from your own homeland as well.
en.R: The king said to Ittai, the man from Gath, "Why are you coming with us? Go back and stay with the new king. You are a foreigner, far away from your own country.

decisions.choice: Ittai the Gittite: a Philistine soldier from Gath
decisions.reason: Gath was one of the five Philistine cities (1 Samuel 6:17). Ittai had come over to David with his men and their families (verse 22). He later commands a third of David's army (18:2).

decisions.choice: the king: Absalom, now proclaimed king
decisions.reason: David speaks of Absalom as "the king", the one now proclaimed in Hebron (verse 10). He may say it with some bitterness, but the point is that Ittai, a foreigner, owes no loyalty to one side in Israel's quarrel and could serve whoever reigns.

decisions.choice: a foreigner and an exile from your place: one far from his own homeland
decisions.reason: Ittai is a foreigner and also an exile, someone who has left his own country. "To your place" is most likely "with respect to your place", that is, far from home. It may also be read with "return": "go back to your own place".

decisions.choice: the new king
decisions.reason: Readable adds "new" so that the reader knows David means Absalom (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the man from Gath
decisions.reason: Readable explains "Gittite".

source.text: תְּמ֣וֹל׀בּוֹאֶ֗ךָ וְהַיּ֞וֹם אֲנִֽיעֲךָ֤ עִמָּ֨נוּ֙ לָלֶ֔כֶת וַאֲנִ֣י הוֹלֵ֔ךְ עַ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־אֲנִ֖י הוֹלֵ֑ךְ שׁ֣וּב וְהָשֵׁ֧ב אֶת־אַחֶ֛יךָ עִמָּ֖ךְ חֶ֥סֶד וֶאֱמֶֽת׃

records.literal_gloss: Yesterday [was] your coming, and today shall I make you wander with us to go, and I [am] going where I [am] going? Return and take back your brothers with you; steadfast love and faithfulness.

en.L: Yesterday [was] your coming, and today shall I make you wander with us, to go, while I am going wherever I go? Return, and take back your brothers with you; steadfast love and faithfulness [be with you]."
en.B: You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander about with us today, when I do not even know where I am going? Go back, and take your kinsmen with you. May faithful love and faithfulness go with you."
en.R: You came here only yesterday. Should I make you wander around with us today? I do not even know where I am going! Go back, and take your people with you. May faithful love and loyalty be with you."

decisions.choice: yesterday: only a short time ago
decisions.reason: "Yesterday" means recently, not literally the day before (compare Exodus 5:14). Ittai had not served David long.

decisions.choice: shall I make you wander: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell the verb in a slightly different form, and the reading noted by the scribes in the margin gives the usual causative form, "make you wander". The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: I am going wherever I go: I do not know where I am going
decisions.reason: The repeated verb leaves the destination open, as in 1 Samuel 23:13. David has no fixed refuge and cannot promise Ittai anything.

decisions.choice: steadfast love and faithfulness: as a blessing on Ittai
alternatives: and may the LORD show you steadfast love and faithfulness
decisions.reason: The Hebrew ends with the bare words "steadfast love and faithfulness", a short blessing: may these go with you. The Greek translation reads "and may the LORD show you steadfast love and faithfulness", as in 2:6. Either way David blesses Ittai with the loyal kindness that Ittai is showing to him (verse 21). The pair of words is used of God's faithful care (Exodus 34:6) and of loyalty between people (Genesis 47:29).

decisions.choice: your brothers: your fellow men from Gath
decisions.reason: "Brothers" means Ittai's own people, the men and families who came with him (verses 18, 22).

decisions.choice: kinsmen (Readable: people)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid "brothers", since Ittai's companions were not his brothers by birth.

decisions.choice: May faithful love and faithfulness go with you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the wish that the bare nouns imply, as Literal does with brackets. As elsewhere, steadfast love is "faithful love" at Balanced and Readable; Readable says "loyalty" for the second word to avoid repeating "faithful".

decisions.choice: I do not even know where I am going!
decisions.reason: Readable gives David's question as two sentences.

source.text: וַיַּ֧עַן אִתַּ֛י אֶת־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר חַי־יְהוָ֗ה וְחֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּ֠י אִם־בִּמְק֞וֹם אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִֽהְיֶה־שָּׁ֣ם׀אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ אִם־לְמָ֨וֶת֙ אִם־לְחַיִּ֔ים כִּי־שָׁ֖ם יִהְיֶ֥ה עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Ittai the king and said, [As] lives Yahweh and [as] lives my lord the king, surely in [the] place where will be there my lord the king, whether for death or for life, surely there will be your servant.

en.L: And Ittai answered the king and said, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, and [as] my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king will be, whether for death or for life, there your servant will surely be."
en.B: But Ittai replied to the king, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, and by the life of my lord the king, in whatever place my lord the king may be, whether it means death or life, there your servant will be."
en.R: But Ittai answered the king, "I make a solemn promise, as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives and as you live, my lord the king: wherever you go, your servant will go too. If it means I die, or if I live, I will be with you."

decisions.choice: as the LORD lives: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: An oath "as the LORD lives" calls on the living God as witness (1 Samuel 14:39; 20:3). Ittai, a foreigner, swears by the God of Israel and adds an oath by the life of the king, as people did at court (1 Samuel 17:55).

decisions.choice: wherever my lord the king is, there your servant will be: loyalty to death
decisions.reason: Ittai's answer is the faithful love David has just wished on him (verse 20). It sounds like Ruth's promise to Naomi (Ruth 1:16-17): a foreigner binding himself to Israel's king and Israel's God whatever comes. His loyalty stands against the betrayal by David's own son and counselor.

decisions.choice: surely: the oath formula
decisions.reason: The written text has the words "surely if" (the usual way of introducing what one swears to), while the scribes' note in the margin reads only "surely". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: your servant: polite self-reference
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, Ittai calls himself "your servant", but here the words also state his loyalty.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, "your servant" is kept at every level.

decisions.choice: wherever you go, your servant will go too. If it means I die, or if I live, I will be with you
decisions.reason: Readable says "I make a solemn promise" to show that this is an oath, speaks to the king as "you", and splits the long promise into shorter sentences.

source.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר דָּוִ֛ד אֶל־אִתַּ֖י לֵ֣ךְ וַעֲבֹ֑ר וַֽיַּעֲבֹ֞ר אִתַּ֤י הַגִּתִּי֙ וְכָל־אֲנָשָׁ֔יו וְכָל־הַטַּ֖ף אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said David to Ittai, Go and pass on. And passed on Ittai the Gittite and all his men and all the little ones who [were] with him.

en.L: And David said to Ittai, "Go and pass on." And Ittai the Gittite passed on, and all his men and all the little ones who [were] with him.
en.B: David said to Ittai, "Go ahead, then, and march on." So Ittai the Gittite marched on with all his men and all the families who were with him.
en.R: So David said to Ittai, "Then come along with us." Ittai and all his men went on ahead, together with all their families and children.

decisions.choice: go and pass on: David accepts Ittai's loyalty
decisions.reason: David no longer sends Ittai back but lets him cross over and march on with the king's company, past the point where David stood (verse 18).

decisions.choice: the little ones: the children and the households
decisions.reason: The word means small children, and often the whole dependent family that traveled with the fighting men (Numbers 32:16-17; Deuteronomy 1:39). Ittai and his men had brought their families with them into exile.

decisions.choice: Then come along with us
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of David's permission, since "pass on" here means joining the march.

decisions.choice: families; families and children
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "families" for the "little ones", which here means the dependents who came with the men.

source.text: וְכָל־הָאָ֗רֶץ בּוֹכִים֙ ק֣וֹל גָּד֔וֹל וְכָל־הָעָ֖ם עֹֽבְרִ֑ים וְהַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עֹבֵר֙ בְּנַ֣חַל קִדְר֔וֹן וְכָל־הָעָם֙ עֹבְרִ֔ים עַל־פְּנֵי־דֶ֖רֶךְ אֶת־הַמִּדְבָּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And all the land [were] weeping [with a] loud voice, and all the people [were] passing on; and the king [was] passing over in the Wadi Kidron, and all the people [were] passing on toward [the] way of the wilderness.

en.L: And all the land [was] weeping with a loud voice, and all the people [were] passing on; and the king [was] crossing the Wadi Kidron, and all the people [were] passing on toward the way of the wilderness.
en.B: The whole countryside wept aloud as all the people passed by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people went on toward the road to the wilderness.
en.R: Everyone in the countryside cried loudly as the people went by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and the people moved on toward the desert road.

decisions.choice: all the land was weeping: the people of the countryside
decisions.reason: "The land" stands for the people who lived in it, as in Genesis 41:57. They wept as they watched their king leave.

decisions.choice: the Wadi Kidron: the valley east of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: A wadi is a valley with a stream that flows only in the rainy season. The Kidron runs between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. To cross it was to leave the city behind (1 Kings 2:37).

decisions.choice: toward the way of the wilderness: the road east to the Jordan
decisions.reason: The road led over the Mount of Olives into the dry country of Judah and down to the Jordan valley (verse 28; 17:16, 22).

decisions.choice: passing on; crossing: the same verb, repeated
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses one verb, "pass over", five times in verses 22-24 and again in verse 33. The repetition marks the long procession out of the city and over the valley.

decisions.choice: Kidron Valley
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "valley" for "wadi", the word most readers know; Literal keeps "wadi".

source.text: וְהִנֵּ֨ה גַם־צָד֜וֹק וְכָֽל־הַלְוִיִּ֣ם אִתּ֗וֹ נֹֽשְׂאִים֙ אֶת־אֲרוֹן֙ בְּרִ֣ית הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים וַיַּצִּ֨קוּ֙ אֶת־אֲר֣וֹן הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים וַיַּ֖עַל אֶבְיָתָ֑ר עַד־תֹּ֥ם כָּל־הָעָ֖ם לַעֲב֥וֹר מִן־הָעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And look, also Zadok, and all the Levites with him carrying [the] ark of [the] covenant of God; and they set down [the] ark of God, and went up Abiathar, until had finished all the people passing out from the city.

en.L: And look, Zadok also [came], and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God; and they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up, until all the people had finished passing out from the city.
en.B: Zadok was there too, with all the Levites carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set the ark of God down, and Abiathar went up, while the people finished leaving the city.
en.R: Zadok the priest was there too, and all the Levites with him were carrying the ark of God's covenant. They put the ark down, and Abiathar went up, until all the people had come out of the city.

decisions.choice: Zadok and Abiathar: David's two chief priests
decisions.reason: Zadok and Abiathar served as priests together in David's reign (8:17; 20:25). Abiathar had joined David when Saul killed the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:20-23).

decisions.choice: the ark of the covenant of God: the sacred chest
decisions.reason: The ark held the tablets of the covenant (Deuteronomy 10:1-5). David had brought it to Jerusalem (6:17). The priests bring it out, perhaps to go with the king into battle as in 1 Samuel 4:3-4.

decisions.choice: Abiathar went up: the sense is uncertain
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only that Abiathar "went up". He may have gone up the road or the Mount of Olives, or the verb may stand for "offered up" sacrifices (another form of the same verb is used for offering a burnt offering, 24:22) while the people passed by. The Hebrew is very brief and the sense is not certain.

decisions.choice: set down: placed firmly
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "pour out", but here it means to set something down in place, as in Joshua 7:23.

decisions.choice: was there too
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave out "look" and say that Zadok was there; the word draws attention to his arrival, which "was there too" conveys.

decisions.choice: Zadok the priest
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the priest", as in verse 27, so that Zadok is identified.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְצָד֔וֹק הָשֵׁ֛ב אֶת־אֲר֥וֹן הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים הָעִ֑יר אִם־אֶמְצָ֥א חֵן֙ בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וֶהֱשִׁבַ֕נִי וְהִרְאַ֥נִי אֹת֖וֹ וְאֶת־נָוֵֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king to Zadok, Return [the] ark of God [to] the city; if I find favor in [the] eyes of Yahweh, and he will bring me back and show me it and his dwelling place.

en.L: And the king said to Zadok, "Return the ark of God [to] the city. If I find favor in the eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will bring me back and let me see it and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} dwelling place.
en.B: Then the king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will bring me home again and let me see the ark and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} dwelling place once more.
en.R: Then the king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back to the city. If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is pleased with me, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will bring me back. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will let me see the ark again, and the place where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives.

decisions.choice: return the ark to the city: David will not use the ark to secure God's help
decisions.reason: Israel once carried the ark into battle as if it guaranteed victory, and lost it (1 Samuel 4:3-11). David leaves it in its place and puts his future in the LORD's hands (verse 26), not in the sacred object.

decisions.choice: find favor in the eyes of the LORD: be accepted by him
decisions.reason: To find favor in someone's eyes is to have his goodwill (Genesis 6:8; Exodus 33:12-13). David's return depends on the LORD's will, not on his own plans.

decisions.choice: his dwelling place: the place where the LORD is present with the ark
decisions.reason: The word is used for a pasture or a home (7:8; Exodus 15:13). Here it is the tent in Jerusalem where the ark stood (6:17), and so the city where the LORD has made his dwelling.

decisions.choice: Then he will let me see the ark again, and the place where he lives
decisions.reason: Readable names the ark for "it" and explains "dwelling place" in a separate sentence.

decisions.choice: is pleased with me
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom "find favor in the eyes of".

source.text: וְאִם֙ כֹּ֣ה יֹאמַ֔ר לֹ֥א חָפַ֖צְתִּי בָּ֑ךְ הִנְנִ֕י יַֽעֲשֶׂה־לִּ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר ט֖וֹב בְּעֵינָֽיו׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And if thus he says, Not I delight in you, here I [am]; let him do to me as [is] good in his eyes.

en.L: But if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says thus, 'I have no delight in you,' here I [am]; let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} do to me as [is] good in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes."
en.B: But if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then here I am; let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} deal with me as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sees fit."
en.R: But if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then I am ready. He may do to me whatever {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} thinks is best."

decisions.choice: here I am; let him do to me as seems good to him: David submits to God's will
decisions.reason: "Here I am" is the answer of one ready to accept what comes (1 Samuel 3:18, where Eli says "Let him do what is good in his eyes"). David accepts that his flight may be the LORD's judgment, as Nathan had warned (12:10-12).

decisions.choice: I have no delight in you: I do not accept you
decisions.reason: The verb means to take pleasure in someone or to want him (22:20; 1 Samuel 18:22). The LORD's rejection would mean David would not return.

decisions.choice: He may do to me ...
decisions.reason: In Readable the pronoun for God begins a sentence, so it is capitalized either way and takes no setting span.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־צָד֣וֹק הַכֹּהֵ֔ן הֲרוֹאֶ֣ה אַתָּ֔ה שֻׁ֥בָה הָעִ֖יר בְּשָׁל֑וֹם וַאֲחִימַ֨עַץ בִּנְךָ֜ וִיהוֹנָתָ֧ן בֶּן־אֶבְיָתָ֛ר שְׁנֵ֥י בְנֵיכֶ֖ם אִתְּכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king to Zadok the priest, [Are] seeing you? Return [to] the city in peace, and Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan son of Abiathar, two sons of you, with you.

en.L: And the king said to Zadok the priest, "Do you see? Return to the city in peace, and Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, your two sons, with you.
en.B: The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Do you understand? Go back to the city in peace, and take your two sons with you: your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar.
en.R: The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Do you understand my plan? Go back safely to the city. Take your son Ahimaaz with you, and Abiathar's son Jonathan too.

decisions.choice: Do you see?: do you understand what I intend?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is a short question, "Are you seeing?" David seems to ask whether Zadok grasps his plan: the priests will serve as his eyes and ears in the city (verses 28, 35-36). The same word is also the noun "seer", an old name for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9), and the question can be read "Are you a seer?", or, with a small change, "Are you not a seer?" Zadok is nowhere else called a seer. The Greek translation reads "See, you are going back".

decisions.choice: your two sons: the sons of Zadok and Abiathar
decisions.reason: "Your" is plural: the two sons belong to the two priests, one each. They will carry messages to David (verse 36; 17:17-21).

decisions.choice: in peace: safely
decisions.reason: The phrase means without harm. The priests can go back to the city without suspicion and be safe there.

decisions.choice: take your two sons with you
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no verb for the sons, only "with you". Balanced and Readable supply "take".

decisions.choice: my plan
decisions.reason: Readable adds "my plan" to say what Zadok is to understand. This depends on the reading chosen in m1.

source.text: רְאוּ֙ אָנֹכִ֣י מִתְמַהְמֵ֔הַּ בְּעַֽרְב֖וֹת הַמִּדְבָּ֑ר עַ֣ד בּ֥וֹא דָבָ֛ר מֵעִמָּכֶ֖ם לְהַגִּ֥יד לִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: See, I [will be] waiting at [the] fords of the wilderness until comes word from with you to tell me.

en.L: See, I [will be] waiting at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to tell me."
en.B: Look, I will wait at the fords in the wilderness until word comes from you to let me know what is happening."
en.R: I will wait at the place where people cross the river in the desert. I will stay there until you send me a message to tell me what is going on."

decisions.choice: the fords of the wilderness: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text read "the plains of the wilderness", while the scribes' note in the margin reads "the fords of the wilderness". The two words differ by one similar letter. The fords fit the story better: David waits at the crossing places of the Jordan, and in 17:16, 21-22 he is told to cross over quickly. The plains would be the Jordan valley near those fords, so the place meant is about the same.

decisions.choice: waiting: lingering, delaying
decisions.reason: The verb means to hold back or delay (Genesis 19:16). David will not go farther until he has news.

decisions.choice: the place where people cross the river
decisions.reason: Readable explains "fords".

source.text: וַיָּ֨שֶׁב צָד֧וֹק וְאֶבְיָתָ֛ר אֶת־אֲר֥וֹן הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַיֵּשְׁב֖וּ שָֽׁם׃

records.literal_gloss: And took back Zadok and Abiathar [the] ark of God [to] Jerusalem, and they stayed there.

en.L: And Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back [to] Jerusalem, and they stayed there.
en.B: So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
en.R: So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they stayed there.

decisions.choice: they stayed there: the priests remain in Jerusalem, as David asked
decisions.reason: The priests and the ark stay in the city, where the priests will act for David (verses 35-36).

decisions.choice: [to] Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The Hebrew names the place without a word for "to"; Literal supplies it in brackets.

source.text: וְדָוִ֡ד עֹלֶה֩ בְמַעֲלֵ֨ה הַזֵּיתִ֜ים עֹלֶ֣ה׀וּבוֹכֶ֗ה וְרֹ֥אשׁ לוֹ֙ חָפ֔וּי וְה֖וּא הֹלֵ֣ךְ יָחֵ֑ף וְכָל־הָעָ֣ם אֲשֶׁר־אִתּ֗וֹ חָפוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ רֹאשׁ֔וֹ וְעָל֥וּ עָלֹ֖ה וּבָכֹֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And David [was] going up on [the] ascent of the olives, going up and weeping, and head to him covered, and he [was] going barefoot; and all the people who [were] with him covered each his head, and went up, going up and weeping.

en.L: And David [was] going up the ascent of the olives, going up and weeping, and his head [was] covered, and he [was] walking barefoot; and all the people who [were] with him covered each his head, and they went up, going up and weeping.
en.B: David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went. His head was covered, and he walked barefoot. All the people with him covered their heads too, and they went up weeping as they climbed.
en.R: David went up the road on the Mount of Olives, crying as he went. He covered his head and walked barefoot to show his grief. All the people with him covered their heads too. They cried as they climbed the hill.

decisions.choice: head covered and barefoot: signs of mourning and shame
decisions.reason: Covering the head was a sign of grief or shame (Esther 6:12; Jeremiah 14:3-4). Going barefoot was a sign of mourning and humiliation (Isaiah 20:2-4; Ezekiel 24:17). The king leaves his city as a mourner.

decisions.choice: the ascent of the olives: the slope of the Mount of Olives
decisions.reason: This is the hill east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley (verse 23), named for its olive trees (Zechariah 14:4).

decisions.choice: going up and weeping: a long, continuing climb
decisions.reason: The repeated verbs describe an action that goes on, step by step; the same words close the verse for the people. The writer slows down to show the grief of the whole company.

decisions.choice: the Mount of Olives
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the familiar name of the hill.

decisions.choice: to show his grief
decisions.reason: Readable adds why David covered his head and went barefoot (meaning decision m1).

source.text: וְדָוִד֙ הִגִּ֣יד לֵאמֹ֔ר אֲחִיתֹ֥פֶל בַּקֹּשְׁרִ֖ים עִם־אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔ד סַכֶּל־נָ֛א אֶת־עֲצַ֥ת אֲחִיתֹ֖פֶל יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And David told, saying, Ahithophel [is] among the conspirators with Absalom. And said David, Make foolish, please, [the] counsel of Ahithophel, Yahweh.

en.L: And [someone] told David, saying, "Ahithophel [is] among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "Make foolish, please, the counsel of Ahithophel, O {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.B: Then David was told, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David prayed, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please turn the advice of Ahithophel into foolishness."
en.R: Someone told David, "Ahithophel has joined Absalom's plot!" So David prayed, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please make Ahithophel's advice foolish."

decisions.choice: someone told David: David was told
decisions.reason: The Hebrew reads "and David told", which does not fit, since David is the one who receives the news. With one small change of vowels or a letter the verb reads "it was told to David", and the sentence makes sense that way. The form of the verb may also be used without a named subject: "someone told".

decisions.choice: make Ahithophel's counsel foolish: David's prayer, which the LORD answers
decisions.reason: Ahithophel's advice was as good as a word from God (16:23). David asks the LORD to turn it to foolishness, and the story shows the answer: Hushai appears at once (verse 32), and later "the LORD had ordained to frustrate the good counsel of Ahithophel" (17:14).

decisions.choice: [someone] told David
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the subject the sentence needs (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: prayed
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "prayed" for "said", since David's words are spoken to the LORD.

source.text: וַיְהִ֤י דָוִד֙ בָּ֣א עַד־הָרֹ֔אשׁ אֲשֶֽׁר־יִשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֥ה שָׁ֖ם לֵאלֹהִ֑ים וְהִנֵּ֤ה לִקְרָאתוֹ֙ חוּשַׁ֣י הָאַרְכִּ֔י קָר֨וּעַ֙ כֻּתָּנְתּ֔וֹ וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל־רֹאשֽׁוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, David coming to the top where he would bow down there to God, and look, to meet him Hushai the Archite, torn his tunic and earth on his head.

en.L: And it happened, as David was coming to the summit, where [people] would bow down to God, that look, Hushai the Archite [came] to meet him, his tunic torn and earth on his head.
en.B: When David reached the summit, where God was worshiped, Hushai the Archite came to meet him there. His robe was torn and there was earth on his head.
en.R: David came to the top of the hill, where people used to worship God. There Hushai the Archite came to meet him. His clothes were torn, and he had dirt on his head to show his sorrow.

decisions.choice: where people would bow down to God: a place of worship on the summit
decisions.reason: The verb describes what was usually done there, so the summit was a known place of worship. It may also mean that David himself bowed down there, praying as he passed.

decisions.choice: Hushai the Archite: from the Archite clan near Bethel
decisions.reason: The Archites lived on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin (Joshua 16:2). Hushai is called "David's friend" (verse 37; 16:16), and he is listed among the king's men in 1 Chronicles 27:33.

decisions.choice: his tunic torn and earth on his head: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: Torn clothes and earth on the head were signs of grief at bad news (1:2; 1 Samuel 4:12).

decisions.choice: look, Hushai came to meet him: the answer to David's prayer begins
decisions.reason: Hushai appears just after David's prayer (verse 31), at the place where God was worshiped. He is the man who will defeat Ahithophel's counsel (17:7-14).

decisions.choice: to show his sorrow
decisions.reason: Readable adds why Hushai had torn his clothes and put dirt on his head.

decisions.choice: [people] would bow down; God was worshiped
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. Literal supplies "people" in brackets; Balanced uses a form without a subject.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ דָּוִ֑ד אִ֚ם עָבַ֣רְתָּ אִתִּ֔י וְהָיִ֥תָ עָלַ֖י לְמַשָּֽׂא׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him David, If you pass on with me, and you will be on me for a burden.

en.L: And David said to him, "If you pass on with me, then you will be a burden on me.
en.B: David told him, "If you go on with me, you will only weigh me down.
en.R: David said to him, "If you come with me, you will only be a burden to me.

decisions.choice: a burden: someone to look after, not a help
decisions.reason: Hushai was probably older (17:8-10 describes the fighters, not him), and in flight he would be one more person to care for. In the city he can do much more for David (verse 34).

decisions.choice: only weigh me down (Balanced); only be a burden (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "only" to bring out the contrast with what Hushai can do in the city (verse 34); Balanced puts "burden" as a verb.

source.text: וְאִם־הָעִ֣יר תָּשׁ֗וּב וְאָמַרְתָּ֤ לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ עַבְדְּךָ֨אֲנִ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶֽהְיֶ֔ה עֶ֣בֶד אָבִ֤יךָ וַֽאֲנִי֙ מֵאָ֔ז וְעַתָּ֖ה וַאֲנִ֣י עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְהֵפַרְתָּ֣ה לִ֔י אֵ֖ת עֲצַ֥ת אֲחִיתֹֽפֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: And if [to] the city you return and say to Absalom, Your servant I will be, the king; servant of your father [was] I from then, and now I [am] your servant; and you will frustrate for me the counsel of Ahithophel.

en.L: But if you return [to] the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; I [was] your father's servant formerly, and now I [will be] your servant,' then you will frustrate for me the counsel of Ahithophel.
en.B: But if you go back to the city and tell Absalom, 'O king, I will be your servant. Before, I was your father's servant, but now I will be yours,' then you can defeat the advice of Ahithophel for me.
en.R: But you can help me by going back to the city. Tell Absalom, 'Your Majesty, I will serve you. I used to serve your father, but now I will serve you.' Then you can work against Ahithophel's advice for me.

decisions.choice: servant: one who serves the king at court
decisions.reason: Hushai is to offer himself as Absalom's servant, an adviser in his court, as he had been David's. The word is the same as in the polite "your servant", but here it means real service to a king.

decisions.choice: frustrate the counsel: break it, make it fail
decisions.reason: The verb means to break or bring to nothing (17:14; Psalm 33:10). Hushai's task is to give Absalom other advice so that Ahithophel's plan is not followed (17:5-14).

decisions.choice: formerly ... and now: a change of masters
decisions.reason: Hushai's words set his old service and his new one side by side. They are a lie told to save David, and they say just what Absalom wants to hear (16:16-19).

decisions.choice: servant (Readable: serve)
decisions.reason: Since this is service to a king, "servant" is used at every level; Readable puts it as the verb "serve".

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable uses the modern form of address to a king for "O king".

source.text: וַהֲל֤וֹא עִמְּךָ֙ שָׁ֔ם צָד֥וֹק וְאֶבְיָתָ֖ר הַכֹּהֲנִ֑ים וְהָיָ֗ה כָּל־הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר תִּשְׁמַע֙ מִבֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ תַּגִּ֕יד לְצָד֥וֹק וּלְאֶבְיָתָ֖ר הַכֹּהֲנִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And not with you there [are] Zadok and Abiathar the priests? And it will be, every word that you hear from [the] house of the king, you will tell to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests.

en.L: And [are] not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So it will be that every word that you hear from the king's house, you will tell to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests.
en.B: Zadok and Abiathar the priests will be there with you, will they not? Tell them everything you hear from the king's palace.
en.R: The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there with you. Tell them everything you hear in the palace.

decisions.choice: are not ... with you?: a question that means "they are with you"
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer yes. David reminds Hushai that he will not be alone in the city.

decisions.choice: the king's house: the palace, where Absalom will hold court
decisions.reason: "The king" now means Absalom, who will take over the palace (16:15, 21).

decisions.choice: will be there with you (statement)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the question as the statement it implies.

records.literal_gloss: Look, there with them [are] their two sons, Ahimaaz of Zadok and Jonathan of Abiathar; and you will send by their hand to me every word that you hear.

en.L: Look, their two sons [are] there with them, Ahimaaz [son] of Zadok and Jonathan [son] of Abiathar; and you will send to me by them every word that you hear."
en.B: Their two sons are there with them, Zadok's son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan. Send them to me with everything you hear."
en.R: Their sons are there with them too: Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son. Send them to me with everything you find out."

decisions.choice: send by their hand: send messages through them
decisions.reason: "By the hand of" means by means of someone, here as messengers. The plan works in 17:15-22, where the two young men carry Hushai's warning to David.

decisions.choice: Ahimaaz of Zadok: Zadok's son Ahimaaz
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "Ahimaaz to Zadok", meaning the son belonging to Zadok, as verse 27 makes clear.

decisions.choice: (no word for "look")
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave "look" unsaid; it points to the young men, which the plain statement already does.

records.literal_gloss: And came Hushai, friend of David, [to] the city, and Absalom came [to] Jerusalem.

en.L: And Hushai, David's friend, came [to] the city, and Absalom came [to] Jerusalem.
en.B: So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
en.R: So David's friend Hushai went back into the city. He got there just as Absalom was arriving in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: David's friend: perhaps a court title, the king's friend
decisions.reason: "The king's friend" was an office at court, a trusted adviser (1 Kings 4:5; 1 Chronicles 27:33, where Hushai is "the king's friend"). Here it may be both a title and a statement of personal loyalty, which Absalom later questions (16:16-17).

decisions.choice: and Absalom came: at the same moment
decisions.reason: The two clauses set the arrivals side by side: Hushai reaches the city just as Absalom enters it. The story goes on from here in 16:15.

decisions.choice: just as
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "just as" to bring out the timing that the paired clauses imply (meaning decision m2).
